subtitle: The Most Powerful Factor in Asia: The Buyback Factor
title: Juicing The Market, One Repurchase at a Time

In Buybacks We Trust.

Asian equities have long been considered value traps, and it’s not hard to see why. Over the last 20 years, the HSI (Hong Kong), Topix (Japan), and Straits Times Index (Singapore) have underperformed the S&P 500 by a significant margin.

Much of this differential is due to the US’s superior economic expansion and the S&P’s incredible earnings growth, but an often under-discussed piece of the puzzle is capital management.

American companies are ruthless when it comes to using financial engineering to maximize shareholder value.

Take Transdigm, for example. Not only does the company operate with negative equity and leverage of 3.8x ($17 B of net debt on $4.7 B of EBITDA), they announced plans today to borrow an additional $5 Billion to fund a “special dividend”. This would cause the average Japanese or HK CEO a heart attack, but to an American, it’s just business as usual.

Recent regulatory reforms and government initiatives are pressuring more and more companies in South Korea, Japan, Singapore, and China to be more active on the capital management front. Many of these countries have observed how the United States and Australia have turned their markets into perpetual wealth machines by encouraging active capital management and passive investment by the public, and are eager to emulate this for themselves. This gets me interested, especially given that all Asian indices trade at a steep discount to the S&P 500 despite having near-zero interest rates (making it easier to buy on margin).

The Asian regulatory push for active capital management is commendable, but it also overshadows a select few companies who don’t need to be told: they’ve been doing the right thing for decades.

Before we go further, don’t look at the legend on the graph below, and try to guess what the chart is of.

Is this the equity curve of an advanced quantitative strategy, a multistrategy hedge fund, or the average life of a tech investor? Guess again.

It’s the active performance graph of the share repurchase factor within Asian equity indices.

The share repurchase factor is simple: rank all index components in descending order by percentage of outstanding shares repurchased within the last 12 months. This graph outlines the outperformance relative to the index if you went long the top quintile of the repurchase factor (20% of the list) relative to the benchmark.

Whether you look at the HSI, BBG APAC, or Topix, the result couldn’t be more clear: repurchasers outperform.

There are many reasons why this is the case. For starters, buybacks tend to separate real operators from those that are cooking their books; it’s extremely rare for frauds (frequently on HKEX) to have the cash to meaningfully repurchase stock. Additionally, buybacks practically serve as a filter on cash flow, capex intensive, struggling, businesses simply don’t have the capacity to repurchase stock. Finally, and perhaps most importantly, buybacks are indicative of whether a company is truly being run for the benefit of shareholders.

Japan and Hong Kong are rife with subsidiary listings or closely held companies where cash is siphoned to related parties of the insiders, or worse, used for low return M&A so executives can pursue an ill-conceived power trip. The last thing these guys tend to do is return cash to the shareholders, so the presence and execution of a buyback almost always removes these types of companies from a buyback factor strategy.

This isn’t to say that any Asian company with a buyback is unquestionably better than peers, or that a company without a buyback can’t be a winning position for you. Of course, anything is possible.

Still, Asian value investing hinges equally on forecasting earnings and assessing whether profits will actually be returned to shareholders. Who wants to own something at 4x earnings if you’ll never see a dime of the cash? In this context, the presence and execution of a buyback has huge signaling value in Asia. It shows management is serious about capital allocation and is committed to maximizing shareholder value.

The results clearly show that the deck is stacked in favor of repurchasers - if there is one thing you takeaway from this article let it be this: the buyback factor works in Asia.

Given a value screen in Japan or Hong Kong can turn up hundreds if not thousands of results, why not add in a screen for buybacks to help refine your list?

Screening.

It’s important to contextualize Asian buybacks with overall capital returns. Baby steps are fine; if a company pays a 4% dividend and starts repurchasing 2-3% of shares outstanding a year, I’m interested.

I prefer names that execute a repurchase in a slow-and-steady manner. A few Japanese and Hong Kong names like to announce sizeable 5-10% buybacks that lead to an immediate pop, but ultimately these maneuvers lead to an unfavorable repurchase execution and the moves tend to fade quickly.

For example, Itoki 7972 announced it would repurchase 10% of shares in a block transaction in February of 2024. The price spiked 33% within two days (leading to an unfavorable repurchase price), and the stock retraced the entire move over the next twelve months.

Screening for repurchases is simple on Bloomberg. My rule of thumb is to add a repurchase filter within my screen for names that have bought back at least 2% of outstanding shares within the last 12 months.

You can accomplish this on EQS by inputting Shares Outstanding as of the Latest Filing on the first line, is less than or equal to Shares Outstanding 4 Quarters ago x 0.98 on the second line (When you input Shares Outstanding in the second line, give it a few seconds, and then click the dropdown arrow to the right of Latest Filing on the second line, then select customize period).

If you want to filter for companies that have repurchased 3%, replace 0.98 vs 0.97, etc. Of course, you can also change the revelavant time frame by selecting Q-8, etc. Unfortunately, this method will exclude any names that have repurchased shares and also conducted a stock split, but by and large it gets the job done.

It’s pretty easy to screen for share repurchasers on Koyfin as well. Although Koyfin doesn’t allow for custom formulas when screening, there is a simple workaround.

If you are screening for companies in the 500 Million to 1 Billion Market Cap range who have repurchased at least 2% of Shares Outstanding, you just need to do some mental math. Any company that fits this criteria would have spent at least 10 Million on repurchases, so select the Repurchase of Common Stock Field and set the lower bound to -999,999 Million and the upper bound to -10 Million.

If you are looking for names in the 5 Billion to 10 Billion Market Cap range who have repurchased at least 2% of shares, you’ll need to modify the upper bound to -100 Million.

You shouldn’t blindly jump into a company due to the mere presence of a share repurchase program. Nonetheless, if you have two equally compelling setups with similar fundamentals at a similar valuation, why not go for the repurchaser? The repurchase program itself skews the risk-to-reward of the trade since the company is actively supporting the stock price, and furthermore, the data shows that Asian share repurchasers tend to significantly outperform the broader index. Now, let’s get into two names that have caught my eye.

Putting It Together

I’ve been increasing my exposure to Asia. I think the tailwind of passive investment and capital management is beneficial to the indices overall, and I’ve been focusing on names with a global presence that trade at depressed, local valuations.

Modern Dental Group (3600:HKEX)

Price: $4.62 HKD

Trailing P/E: 10.5x

Forward P/E: 9.2x

5 Year Revenue CAGR: 6.9%

5 Year EPS CAGR: 20.3%

Dividend: 4%

Buyback Yield: 2%

Insider Ownership: 67%

Modern Dental Group is a leading global manufacturer of dental prosthetics and implants, operating a network of 80 labs across Europe, the United States, Australia, and China. Despite its Hong Kong HQ, only 19% of revenue is China-based; its largest segments are Europe (48% of revenue under its Labocast, Permadental, and Elysee brands) and North America (22% of revenue under its Modern Dental and Microdental brands).

The company has steadily grown its global footprint with the acquisition of Microdental in the United States (2016), Dentrade in Norway (2017), DD Dental Gmbh in Germany (2019), ApexDigital in Malaysia (2022) and most recently Hexa Ceram in Thailand (2025). Modern Dental operates off a direct-to-dentist model, cutting out costly middlemen and distributors, enabling dentists to place direct orders from local labs that operate under regional Modern Dental Group’s regional subsidiaries.

I like this approach, as it enables Modern Dental Group to avoid a “Chinese Company” stigma (which honestly shouldn’t apply anyways since dental implants like crowns and bridges are milled in local laboratories). By standardizing offerings, production, and supply chains while maintaining a local “feel”, Modern Dental Group has been able to rapidly expand in Europe and the United States, which has significantly lowered its reliance on China as a source of revenue and income.

I’m attracted to Modern Dental for Four Reasons: Insider Alignment, Capital Management, Prospects for Future Growth, and the Current Valuation.

Modern Dental’s two founders, the Chan and Ngai Families, own 67% of the company (600 Million shares, $350 Million US) and have not sold a single share within the last 10 years. Their high level of alignment, and Modern Dental Group’s consistent dividends and repurchases alongside expansion seem to indicate the company is run for the benefit of the shareholders (overall executive compensation is just 4 Million).

I’m especially impressed by Modern Dental Group’s capital management. The dividend has steadily increased from $0.045 HKD in 2019, to $0.081 HKD in 2022, $0.104 HKD in 2023, $0.17 HKD in 2024, to what will likely be $0.172 HKD this year.

The company has also amplified its buyback efforts, repurchasing approximately 10 Million shares (1% of outstanding, 3% of the float) year to date. While the repurchases may seem small, given the high level of insider ownership and limited trading volume and float, I think it sends a strong signal the company finds its shares attractive in the $4.00 - $4.50 HKD range. The company is currently in a blackout period as results will be reported later this month, but in May, June, and July, buybacks amounted to 100,000 shares a day (0.03% of the float), nearly 20% of the average daily volume.

It’s rare to see a company in Asia with such high insider ownership engage in buybacks of this level while also paying a sizeable dividend and pursuing expansion. I think the presence of the buyback signals management’s confidence in the company, and is also highly accretive to future earnings given where the stock is trading.

I like Modern Dental Group’s prospects for future growth. Local dental labs are a highly fragmented market. Modern Dental Group has consistently gained a foothold by acquiring mid-sized lab networks in foreign countries, and then growing their network by acquiring smaller, single labs. The $20 Million acquisition of Hexa Ceram in Thailand seems to indicate there is still global opportunity, and Modern Dental Group’s new focus on digital scanning techniques to boost profit margins and narrow fulfillment times from 11 to 8 days indicates it is highly competitive. Despite its strong earnings performance over the past 5 years, I think recent acquisitions and organic growth can propel earnings to record levels.

I find the stock attractive at just 10x earnings given the dividend, capital returns, and track record of growth. Given the inherent risks of small cap investing in Hong Kong and the earnings report later this month, I’ve sized the position small at 0.5%. Nonetheless, Modern Dental Group is a global player trading at a depressed, local valuation despite its excellent capital management and consistent expansion. It would undoubtedly be trading at a much higher multiple if it was listed in the United States or Europe, which is even more ironic given nearly 80% of revenues are from the US and EU.

I find the stock attractive in the $4.20 - $4.60 range (where the company was repurchasing shares), and if 1H results are strong I plan on increasing my position.

I’ll keep the second pitch brief, since it’s a bank and no one ever finds these interesting.

Bank of the Ryukyus (8399:TYO)

Price: ¥ 1268

Trailing P/E: 9.4x

Forward P/E: 8.0x

Price to Tangible Book Value: 0.37x

Dividend: 3%

Buyback Yield: 1%

Bank of the Ryukyus is a Japanese regional bank in the Okinawa Prefecture, established by the US Military in 1948 to restore financial order.

The company recently graduated to the Tokyo Stock Exchange “Prime” Segment, which demands investor friendly disclosures and higher standards for capital management. Ryukyus is a significant beneficiary of the higher interest rate environment: a mere 12 bps expansion in its Net Interest Margin is set to propel earnings from ¥ 136 to ¥ 154 .

Treasury Secretary Bessent has been applying pressure on the BOJ to raise rates, both as a nudge to tackle inflation, and also as an element of US Trade Policy to strengthen the Yen.

Bessent isn’t alone, Japanese executives themselves have been demanding rate hikes (although in the case of banking executives, it’s pretty clear why).

“Japan’s central bank should raise rates when its policy board meets this week, and failure to do so will weaken the yen and exacerbate inflation, said Takeshi Niinami, chief executive officer of Suntory Holdings Ltd”

As a result, Japan’s 10-Year bond yield is hovering near the highest levels since the early 2010’s, and short-term interest rate derivatives imply the Bank of Japan will conduct a 25 basis point hike by next March.

For someone like Bank of the Ryukyus with a near zero-cost deposit base, this is free money and represents an earnings windfall.

Ever since the August 2024 Japan Meltdown (a slow 5% drawdown followed by a 13% move where the market was halted 3 times), Japanese Regional Banks haven’t recovered while their larger peers have soared to record highs. Larger banks have jumped from their usual 8-9x forward P/E level to upwards of 11x as investors price in rate hike optimism, while smaller banks have languished.

Recently, that has begun to change. The environment is rife for M&A Consolidation and increased capital returns. Smaller Banks like Ryukyus (8399), Juroko (7380), Keiyo (8544) and Mebuki (7167) are beginning to move as the valuation gap closes and fresh 52 week highs prompt renewed attention from shaken-out investors.

I like Ryukyus (and to a lesser extent Juroko) for its strong earnings growth, rapidly improving credit quality, and most importantly its implementation of capital management.

The company has been repurchasing 1-1.5% of shares a year on top of its respectable dividend, and the management team seems to be well aware of the significant discount it trades at relative to Tangible Book Value (.

Ryukyus is standalone attractive at 8x earnings (perhaps 7.5x if another rate hike occurs) as a tactical trade relative to larger Japanese banks, and also as a long term holding predicated on a rising interest rate environment. I think the introduction of a more significant buyback in early 2026 could serve as a positive development, and a more in-line industry P/E of 9.5x would imply a value of ¥ 1,500 a share. It’s important to note management’s own guidance of ¥ 158 this year does not account for further rate hikes. Not only would an additional rate hike boost earnings, even if rates remain constant, earnings will grow as the loan book continues to reprice higher.

I’ve sized my position small at 0.25% since Japanese banks aren’t a “hot topic”. Nonetheless, small cap Japanese banks as a whole are about to ride the tailwind of a rising rate environment, and I think names that are attentive to capital management and actively addressing the discount they trade at, such as Ryukyus, will significantly outperform those who don’t.
